mediaItem.keyStats:
-   2.2 million people in prison in America
-   4.5 million (or 4.8 million as mentioned later) people on probation and parole
-   More Black people under criminal justice supervision than slaves at the height of slavery in the 1850s/60s.
-   70% of people who return to jail/prison do so for technical probation violations.
-   In Philadelphia, police force increased by 69% decade over decade.
-   California at one point spent more on incarceration than education.
-   US incarcerates 5-9 times more people per capita than Western Europe and 14 times more than Japan.
-   More people in prison for drugs in the US than total prison population in Western Europe.
-   In 1990, 1 in 4 Black children born had an imprisoned father by age 14.
-   30% of Black men without college education will have been to prison by their thirties.
-   60% of Black men without high school education will spend a year in prison or jail before their thirtieth birthday.
-   Pennsylvania is one of three states with no cap on probation.
-   $80 billion a year spent on incarceration in the US.
mediaItem.itemTitle: Jason Flom and Michael Rubin with Meek Mill
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of "Wrongful Conviction with Jason Flom" features Meek Mill and Michael Rubin discussing Meek's wrongful conviction case and the broader systemic issues within the American criminal justice system. Meek recounts his experiences growing up in poverty and being caught in a system that seemed designed to incarcerate young Black men.  Rubin, initially unaware of these disparities, shares his awakening to the two Americas after witnessing Meek's legal battles. The conversation highlights unreliable eyewitness identification, excessive probation terms, the cycle of re-incarceration for technical violations, and the disproportionate impact on communities of color.  They emphasize the need for criminal justice reform, voting, and rethinking punishment to fit the crime, advocating for rehabilitation and addressing systemic flaws instead of perpetuating cycles of poverty and incarceration. The guests call for empathy, common sense solutions, and encourage listeners to get involved in reform efforts.

featuredIndividual.convictionYear: Original wrongful conviction around age 18 (approximately 2005 based on current age of 31 mentioned in transcript as of recording).
featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Not fully exonerated as of the podcast recording; still ongoing legal battles and probation.
featuredIndividual.crimeConvictedOf: Originally charged with pointing a gun at multiple police officers.
featuredIndividual.sentence: Probation (Initially, then re-incarcerated multiple times for probation violations). Original sentence and specific terms not detailed in this transcript but probation and re-incarcerations are repeatedly mentioned.
featuredIndividual.timeServed: Multiple periods of incarceration over 13 years due to original conviction and probation violations. Specific time served for each instance not detailed.
contributingFactorsRaw: Systemic bias against young Black men.
Technical probation violations leading to re-incarceration.
featuredIndividual.status: Still on probation and fighting the original conviction as of the podcast recording. Not fully exonerated.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Not explicitly mentioned in transcript, but implied support from criminal justice reform advocates and potentially organizations working with Michael Rubin. Innocence Project mentioned as a cause Jason Flom supports generally.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Likely appears in exoneree databases due to the discussion of wrongful conviction, but not explicitly confirmed in the transcript.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Meek was arrested and convicted for allegedly pointing a gun at multiple police officers during an arrest.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Not detailed in transcript, but implied that defense was insufficient given the wrongful conviction.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Affidavit from one of the arresting police officers stating that Meek did not point a gun at them, contradicting the initial charges.  However, this evidence has not yet led to full exoneration as of the podcast.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Not applicable as the case is about whether Meek committed the alleged act, not misidentification of perpetrator.

keyQuotesRaw: Meek Mill: "I'm not innocent to approve and guilty, I'm guilty until I approve my innocence and that's absolutely what happened to me."
Meek Mill: "Our system, since I've been out 10 years, it's come a little ways, but it's still broken."
Michael Rubin: "There's two Americans." and later "You were right. I was wrong. And there is two worlds."
Michael Rubin on probation violations: "This is lunacy. This is absolute lunacy."

Meek Mill on prison conditions: "When I say shackled up in the cage, I mean like shackled real chains. When you take a baby step is cutting your legs and like the same thing you see in the slavery movie, it's the same thing."

Robert Kraft (recounted by Michael Rubin): "How are you so happy? ... last time I was with you, we were on a plane flying to an all-star game and you were on the top of the world. Now you're in an orange jumpsuit, locked in prison. You've got a smile from me. You're going to ear to ear." Meek Mill's response: "This is the first time people are actually fighting for me. And that makes me so happy."
systemicIssuesRaw: Racial bias in policing and the justice system.
Over-policing and mass incarceration in impoverished communities.
Lack of rehabilitation focus in the system.
Two-tiered justice system based on wealth and race.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Criminal justice reform - breaking and rebuilding the system.
Voting in local and national elections, especially for DAs and judges who support reform.
Eliminating excessive probation and probation violations as a primary cause of re-incarceration.
Focus on rehabilitation and addressing root causes of crime (poverty, drug addiction).
Advocating for punishment to fit the crime.
Supporting organizations like the Innocence Project.
personalNarrativeRaw: Meek Mill's personal experience of wrongful conviction and ongoing legal battles.  His loss of trust in humanity and the system, but also finding hope in advocacy and support.  His resilience and dedication to criminal justice reform despite personal suffering. His description of the psychological impact of living under constant threat of re-incarceration and the dehumanizing conditions of prison.
Michael Rubin's transformation from disbelief to active advocacy after witnessing Meek's case firsthand. His commitment to using his resources and platform to fight for reform.
additionalResourcesRaw: Book: "On the Run: Fugitive Life in an American City" by Alice Goffman
